newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia PM's cash pledge fails to please parliament.
newsitem.headline: Russia PM's cash pledge fails to please parliament.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, facing strikes and discontent, pledged on Tuesday to pay a huge backlog of unpaid wages and pensions soon but failed to appease the upper house of parliament.

"The government action is inadequate to the situation in the country and the society," the Federation Council said in a non-binding resolution after Chernomyrdin outlined his economic plans to the upper chamber.
"The Federation Council asks the president (Boris Yeltsin) to take radical measures immediately to provide more efficient work by the government in social-economic development."

The resolution was another blow to Chernomyrdin, who is also under pressure from the opposition-dominated lower house of parliament over the upaid wages and pensions and faces a nationwide coalminers' strike.
Some servicemen have also not been paid for months, prompting talk of discontent in the army, although Defence Minister Igor Rodionov has dismissed talk of an army mutiny.
In his speech to the Federation Council, Chernomyrdin promised to pay wage arrears amounting to 7.9 trillion roubles later this month.

Promises to settle the wage and pensions debts have proved empty in the past. Chernomyrdin did not specify where the money would come from, but he said Russia's many regions would get fewer funds from Moscow.

"In all main spheres, except the army, 100 percent of debts will be repaid in December. This way we will make our debts disappear and will not allow new indebtedness to form and grow," Chernomyrdin said.
He did not explain why the army, which has no right to strike, would not be paid.
But he said the government planned to repay all debts on pensions and start regular monthly pension payments next year.

The Federation Council, traditionally compliant to the demands of Yeltsin and his government, last week demanded that the government explain its failure to pay the months of back wages owed to workers in the public sector.
Chernomyrdin earned the chamber's wrath by ignoring a plea to address it last week.
The wage arrears provoked the nationwide coalminers' strike, which started last week and prompted sporadic protests in various parts of the country.

Suggestions by Chernomyrdin that the regions will not get their full budget subsidies this year because they owe money to Moscow could further antagonise the upper chamber, which is made up of regional leaders.

The prime minister stood by his draft 1997 budget, which has been criticised by the opposition communists in the State Duma, the lower house. The Duma will vote whether to approve the budget next Sunday.

The budget must be approved by the Duma and the Federation Council before Yeltsin can sign it into law. If deputies fail to approve a new budget by the end of the year, Russia will have to adopt interim budgets or use the 1996 law again.
